stimuli.title: U.S. Constitution, Article V (1787)
stimuli.html: The Congress, whenever two thirds of both Houses shall deem it necessary, shall propose Amendments to this Constitution, or, on the Application of the Legislatures of two thirds of the several States, shall call a Convention for proposing Amendments, which, in either Case, shall be valid to all Intents and Purposes, as Part of this Constitution, when ratified by the Legislatures of three fourths of the several States, or by Conventions in three fourths thereof, as the one or the other Mode of Ratification may be proposed by the Congress; Provided that no Amendment which may be made prior to the Year One thousand eight hundred and eight shall in any Manner affect the first and fourth Clauses in the Ninth Section of the first Article; and that no State, without its Consent, shall be deprived of its equal Suffrage in the Senate.
stimuli.source: Article V of the Constitution of the United States, signed September 17, 1787

stimuli.title: The Twenty-second Amendment (1951)
stimuli.html:
Congress proposed the Twenty-second Amendment in March 1947, and the states ratified it in February 1951.

Section 1. No person shall be elected to the office of the President more than twice, and no person who has held the office of President, or acted as President, for more than two years of a term to which some other person was elected President shall be elected to the office of the President more than once. But this Article shall not apply to any person holding the office of President when this Article was proposed by the Congress, and shall not prohibit any person who may be holding the office of President, or acting as President, during the term within which this Article becomes operative from holding the office of President or acting as President during the remainder of such term.
stimuli.source: Amendment XXII, Section 1, Constitution of the United States

stimuli.title: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 (excerpts)
stimuli.html:
Title II, Section 201(a)

All persons shall be entitled to the full and equal enjoyment of the goods, services, facilities, privileges, advantages, and accommodations of any place of public accommodation, as defined in this section, without discrimination or segregation on the ground of race, color, religion, or national origin.

Title VII, Section 703(a)

It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer—

(1) to fail or refuse to hire or to discharge any individual, or otherwise to discriminate against any individual with respect to his compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment, because of such individual's race, color, religion, sex, or national origin . . .

Note: Section 201(b) defines places of public accommodation to include hotels and motels, restaurants and lunch counters, gas stations, movie theaters, and sports arenas.
stimuli.source: Excerpts from the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Public Law 88-352, signed July 2, 1964

stimuli.title: How the Civil Rights Act Became Law
stimuli.html:
(1) In June 1963, President John F. Kennedy asked Congress to pass a broad civil rights law. After Kennedy was assassinated in November 1963, President Lyndon B. Johnson urged Congress to pass the bill. The House of Representatives approved it on February 10, 1964, by a vote of 290 to 130.

(2) In the Senate, opponents of the bill began a filibuster—a long, continuing debate meant to prevent a final vote. Under Senate rules at the time, debate could be ended only by a "cloture" vote of two-thirds of the senators present and voting. After more than two months of debate, on June 10, 1964, the Senate voted 71 to 29 for cloture. It was the first time the Senate had ever ended a filibuster against a civil rights bill. The Senate passed the bill on June 19, and President Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act into law on July 2, 1964.

(3) A court challenge came quickly. The owner of the Heart of Atlanta Motel in Atlanta, Georgia, which refused to rent rooms to Black guests, argued that Congress had no power to tell a private business whom it must serve. The motel stood near two interstate highways, advertised in national magazines, and drew about 75 percent of its guests from outside Georgia. In December 1964, in Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States, the Supreme Court unanimously upheld Title II. The justices reasoned that discrimination by hotels and motels discouraged Black Americans from traveling, which burdened trade and travel among the states, and that Article I of the Constitution gives Congress the power to regulate commerce among the states.

stimuli.title: Political Cartoon (described)
stimuli.html:
The cartoon, titled "The Long Climb," shows a tall staircase inside the U.S. Capitol. The steps are labeled, from bottom to top, "Introduced," "Committee," "House Floor," "Senate Floor," and "President's Desk." At the top of the staircase is a small door marked "LAW."

Dozens of tiny paper figures, each labeled "Bill," are climbing the stairs. At the step labeled "Committee," a wide trapdoor stands open, and most of the paper figures are tumbling through it into a huge bin marked "Never Brought to a Vote." Only two small figures have made it near the top. One of them, sweating and out of breath, says to the other, "Just one more step—if he signs."

stimuli.title: Letter to the Editor
stimuli.html:
To the Editor:

Riverton's city elections are badly broken. Our mayor and city council are chosen in May of odd-numbered years, on a day when no state or national races are on the ballot. In the most recent city election, held last May, only 14 percent of registered voters cast a ballot. That is a shameful number for a city that claims to care about democracy.

A proposal now before the council would move city elections to November of even-numbered years, when many more voters already come to the polls for state and national races. Some residents worry that local races would get lost at the bottom of a long ballot, but I trust Riverton voters to find them. Moving our elections to November would be the smartest decision the council has made in years. Anyone who opposes this change simply does not want ordinary people to vote. The council should approve the proposal at its next meeting.

—A Riverton homeowner
stimuli.source: Letter written for this test; Riverton is a fictional city

stimuli.title: President Andrew Jackson's Message to Congress on Indian Removal (1830)
stimuli.html:
In May 1830, Congress passed the Indian Removal Act, which authorized the President to exchange lands west of the Mississippi River for the homelands of Native American nations in the East. In December 1830, President Andrew Jackson reported to Congress on the policy. The excerpt uses terms of its time that are offensive today.

It gives me pleasure to announce to Congress that the benevolent policy of the Government, steadily pursued for nearly thirty years, in relation to the removal of the Indians beyond the white settlements is approaching to a happy consummation. . . .

The consequences of a speedy removal will be important to the United States, to individual States, and to the Indians themselves. . . . It will place a dense and civilized population in large tracts of country now occupied by a few savage hunters. . . . It will separate the Indians from immediate contact with settlements of whites; free them from the power of the States; enable them to pursue happiness in their own way and under their own rude institutions; will retard the progress of decay, which is lessening their numbers, and perhaps cause them gradually, under the protection of the Government and through the influence of good counsels, to cast off their savage habits and become an interesting, civilized, and Christian community. . . .

What good man would prefer a country covered with forests and ranged by a few thousand savages to our extensive Republic, studded with cities, towns, and prosperous farms embellished with all the improvements which art can devise or industry execute, occupied by more than 12,000,000 happy people, and filled with all the blessings of liberty, civilization and religion?
stimuli.source: Excerpt from President Andrew Jackson's annual message to Congress, December 6, 1830

stimuli.title: The Four Freedoms (1941)
stimuli.html:
President Franklin D. Roosevelt gave this annual message to Congress on January 6, 1941. World War II had been under way in Europe since 1939, and Great Britain was fighting Nazi Germany.

In the future days, which we seek to make secure, we look forward to a world founded upon four essential human freedoms.

The first is freedom of speech and expression—everywhere in the world.

The second is freedom of every person to worship God in his own way—everywhere in the world.

The third is freedom from want—which, translated into world terms, means economic understandings which will secure to every nation a healthy peacetime life for its inhabitants—everywhere in the world.

The fourth is freedom from fear—which, translated into world terms, means a world-wide reduction of armaments to such a point and in such a thorough fashion that no nation will be in a position to commit an act of physical aggression against any neighbor—anywhere in the world.

That is no vision of a distant millennium. It is a definite basis for a kind of world attainable in our own time and generation.
stimuli.source: Excerpt from President Franklin D. Roosevelt's Annual Message to Congress, January 6, 1941

stimuli.title: Eisenhower's Farewell Address (1961)
stimuli.html:
President Dwight D. Eisenhower, a retired five-star Army general who had commanded Allied forces in Europe during World War II, gave this televised address on January 17, 1961, three days before leaving office.

This conjunction of an immense military establishment and a large arms industry is new in the American experience. The total influence—economic, political, even spiritual—is felt in every city, every state house, every office of the Federal government. We recognize the imperative need for this development. Yet we must not fail to comprehend its grave implications. . . .

In the councils of government, we must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence, whether sought or unsought, by the military-industrial complex. The potential for the disastrous rise of misplaced power exists and will persist.

We must never let the weight of this combination endanger our liberties or democratic processes. We should take nothing for granted. Only an alert and knowledgeable citizenry can compel the proper meshing of the huge industrial and military machinery of defense with our peaceful methods and goals, so that security and liberty may prosper together.
stimuli.source: Excerpt from President Dwight D. Eisenhower's Farewell Address, January 17, 1961

items.prompt: According to Article V, a proposed amendment becomes part of the Constitution when it is
options: approved by two-thirds of both houses of Congress
signed into law by the President
ratified by the legislatures of, or conventions in, three-fourths of the states
approved by a majority of voters in a national election
items.explain: Article V says an amendment becomes valid "when ratified by the Legislatures of three fourths of the several States, or by Conventions in three fourths thereof." A two-thirds vote of both houses of Congress only proposes an amendment; it does not add it to the Constitution. Article V gives the President no role, and it does not provide for a national popular vote.

items.prompt: There are 50 states today. Under Article V, what is the smallest number of states that must ratify a proposed amendment for it to become part of the Constitution?
items.explain:
Article V requires ratification by three-fourths of the states.
3/4 × 50 = 37.5
A state cannot ratify halfway, and 37 states would be less than three-fourths (37 ÷ 50 = 74%). So at least 38 states are needed (38 ÷ 50 = 76%). A common error is answering 34, which is two-thirds of 50 rounded up; two-thirds is the fraction for proposing an amendment, not ratifying it.

items.prompt: According to Article V, which are ways an amendment can be proposed? Select two answers.
options: By a two-thirds vote of both houses of Congress
By a national convention that Congress calls when two-thirds of the state legislatures apply for one
By a majority vote of the Supreme Court
By an executive order of the President
By a petition signed by three-fourths of the nation's governors
items.explain: Article V names two methods of proposal: Congress proposes amendments "whenever two thirds of both Houses shall deem it necessary," or, "on the Application of the Legislatures of two thirds of the several States," Congress "shall call a Convention for proposing Amendments." The Supreme Court, the President, and governors have no role in proposing amendments under Article V. (All 27 amendments so far were proposed by Congress.)

items.prompt: A vice president becomes president after the president leaves office with 2 years and 6 months remaining in the term. Under the Twenty-second Amendment, how many times may this person later be elected president?
options: Zero times
One time
Two times
Three times
items.explain: The amendment says that a person who has "held the office of President . . . for more than two years of a term to which some other person was elected President shall be elected to the office of the President more than once." Serving 2 years and 6 months is more than two years of someone else's term, so this person may be elected only one time. If the person had served two years or less of the predecessor's term, he or she could be elected twice. The amendment does not bar the person from running at all, so "zero" is incorrect.

items.skill: Civics: historical context of an amendment
items.prompt: Which development most directly led Congress to propose the Twenty-second Amendment in 1947?
options: Franklin D. Roosevelt had been elected president four times, breaking the two-term tradition begun by George Washington.
The Supreme Court had ruled that presidents could serve only two terms.
Several presidents in a row had refused to leave office when their terms ended.
The states had called a national convention to limit the power of Congress.
items.explain: George Washington chose to step down after two terms, and later presidents followed his example until Franklin D. Roosevelt won elections in 1932, 1936, 1940, and 1944. Two years after his death in office, Congress proposed the Twenty-second Amendment to turn the two-term tradition into a constitutional rule. No Supreme Court ruling set a term limit, no president refused to leave office, and the amendment was proposed by Congress, not a state convention.

items.prompt: Based on the table, which amendment was ratified most quickly after Congress proposed it?
options: The 19th Amendment
The 22nd Amendment
The 24th Amendment
The 26th Amendment
items.explain: The 26th Amendment was proposed and ratified in the same year, 1971 (in fact, in a little over three months). The 19th took from 1919 to 1920, the 24th from 1962 to 1964, and the 22nd from 1947 to 1951.

items.prompt: Which conclusion about the amendment process is best supported by the table?
options: Congress usually ratifies amendments that the states have rejected.
An amendment proposed by Congress does not become part of the Constitution unless enough states ratify it.
Every amendment proposed by Congress is ratified within ten years.
Most amendments in the table changed the powers of the Supreme Court.
items.explain: The Child Labor Amendment was proposed by Congress in 1924 but has never been ratified, so it is not part of the Constitution. This shows that a proposal by Congress is not enough; three-fourths of the states must ratify. The 27th Amendment (proposed 1789, ratified 1992) and the Child Labor Amendment disprove the "ten years" statement. Congress does not ratify amendments, and none of the amendments listed deals with the Supreme Court.

items.skill: Civics: applying a law to cases
items.prompt: Use the excerpts from the Civil Rights Act. Drag each situation into the category that describes it.
choices: A roadside motel refuses to rent rooms to travelers because of their religion.
A factory pays women less than men for the same job because of their sex.
A restaurant refuses to seat customers because of their national origin.
A company refuses to promote an employee because of his race.
A trucking company refuses to hire an applicant who does not have the commercial driver's license the job requires.
items.explain: Title II covers places of public accommodation, such as motels and restaurants, and bars discrimination based on race, color, religion, or national origin. So the motel (religion) and the restaurant (national origin) belong there. Title VII covers employers and bars discrimination in hiring, pay, and promotion based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. So unequal pay because of sex and refusing a promotion because of race belong there. Refusing to hire someone who lacks a required license is not prohibited, because the decision is based on a job qualification, not on any of the listed characteristics.

items.skill: Civics: comparing provisions of a law
items.prompt: Which characteristic is listed as a protected ground in the Title VII excerpt but is not listed in the Title II excerpt?
options: Sex
Religion
National origin
Color
items.explain: Title II lists "race, color, religion, or national origin." Title VII lists "race, color, religion, sex, or national origin." The only ground that appears in Title VII but not in Title II is sex. Religion, national origin, and color appear in both excerpts.

items.skill: Civics: constitutional basis of a law
items.prompt: Which fact about the Heart of Atlanta Motel best supported the Supreme Court's conclusion that Congress had the power to regulate the motel?
options: It was located in Georgia's capital city.
Its owner argued the case himself.
About 75 percent of its guests came from outside Georgia.
It was a privately owned business.
items.explain: The Court upheld Title II under Congress's power to regulate commerce among the states. Because most of the motel's guests were interstate travelers, its practices affected trade and travel between states, which placed it within Congress's commerce power. Being in a capital city or who argued the case has no bearing on that power, and the owner's point that the motel was private was his argument against regulation, not the reason the Court gave for upholding it.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 2, why was the Senate vote on June 10, 1964, a turning point for the civil rights bill?
options: It overrode President Johnson's veto of the bill.
It was the final vote that made the bill a law.
It sent the bill to the House for its first vote.
It ended the filibuster so that the Senate could hold a final vote on the bill.
items.explain: The June 10 vote was a cloture vote, which ended the filibuster that had blocked a final vote. The Senate then passed the bill on June 19, and President Johnson signed it on July 2. Johnson supported the bill and never vetoed it, and the House had already passed the bill in February.

items.skill: Civics: Senate rules and minority power
items.prompt:
Complete the statement.

To end the filibuster in 1964, supporters of the bill needed the votes of {{0}}. The long debate shows that, under Senate rules, a determined minority of senators could {{1}}.

options: a simple majority of senators
two-thirds of the senators present and voting
three-fourths of the state legislatures
the President and the Speaker of the House
delay a vote on a bill that most senators supported
veto a bill that the House had passed
overturn a ruling of the Supreme Court
remove the President from office

items.explain: Paragraph 2 says debate could be ended only by a cloture vote of two-thirds of the senators present and voting; the 71 to 29 vote met that standard (71 ÷ 100 = 71%, more than 66.7%). Because a minority could keep debate going until two-thirds agreed to stop it, opponents were able to delay a vote on a bill that most senators supported for more than two months. Senators cannot veto bills (that is the President's power), overturn Supreme Court rulings, or remove a president by filibustering.

items.prompt: Which president had the greatest percentage of his vetoes overridden by Congress?
options: Franklin D. Roosevelt
Harry S. Truman
Richard M. Nixon
Gerald R. Ford
items.explain:
Divide vetoes overridden by total vetoes:
Roosevelt: 9 ÷ 635 ≈ 1.4%
Truman: 12 ÷ 250 = 4.8%
Nixon: 7 ÷ 43 ≈ 16.3%
Ford: 12 ÷ 66 ≈ 18.2%
Ford had the greatest percentage overridden. Truman and Ford tie for the most overrides (12), but Truman's 12 come out of 250 vetoes, a much smaller share. Roosevelt had the most vetoes but one of the smallest override percentages.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data in the table?
options: Congress overrides only a small share of presidential vetoes, so the veto is a strong check on the legislative branch.
Presidents who served the longest had the highest percentage of vetoes overridden.
Congress overrode most of the vetoes issued by these presidents.
The Supreme Court decided whether each of these vetoes would stand.
items.explain: Altogether the seven presidents issued 1,284 vetoes, and Congress overrode 53 of them, about 4%. Because overriding requires a two-thirds vote in both houses, most vetoes stand, which makes the veto a powerful check by the executive branch on Congress. Roosevelt served longest but had one of the lowest override rates (about 1.4%), and the Supreme Court plays no part in the veto process.

items.prompt: What is the main idea of the cartoon?
options: Bills become law quickly once they are introduced in Congress.
Most bills never become law because the legislative process has many points where a bill can be stopped.
The President introduces most of the bills that Congress considers.
Committees vote to pass most bills that are introduced.
items.explain: The cartoon shows a long staircase of steps a bill must climb, with most bills falling through a trapdoor and only two coming close to the top. The cartoonist's point is that the lawmaking process is long and difficult, so most bills do not become law. The cartoon shows the opposite of quick or easy passage, and members of Congress, not the President, introduce bills.

items.prompt: The trapdoor and the bin marked "Never Brought to a Vote" at the "Committee" step represent which fact about Congress?
options: The President vetoes most bills before they reach Congress.
Bills that fail in the House are automatically sent to the Senate.
Most bills that are introduced stall in committee and are never voted on by the full House or Senate.
Committees are made up of citizens chosen by lottery.
items.explain: After a bill is introduced, it goes to a committee, and most bills are never reported out of committee, so they never get a vote on the floor. The trapdoor at the "Committee" step and the bin labeled "Never Brought to a Vote" show exactly this. The veto happens at the end of the process (the "President's Desk" step), not before Congress acts, and committees are made up of members of Congress.

items.prompt: The sentences below are from the letter. Which sentence could be confirmed by checking official election records? Click that sentence.
spans: Riverton's city elections are badly broken.
In the most recent city election, held last May, only 14 percent of registered voters cast a ballot.
That is a shameful number for a city that claims to care about democracy.
Moving our elections to November would be the smartest decision the council has made in years.
Anyone who opposes this change simply does not want ordinary people to vote.
The council should approve the proposal at its next meeting.
items.explain: Turnout in a past election is a fact: the number of ballots cast and the number of registered voters are public records, so the 14 percent figure can be checked. The other sentences are opinions, signaled by judgment words such as "badly broken," "shameful," "smartest," and "should." The sentence about opponents is also an unfair generalization about people's motives, which cannot be proved.

items.prompt: The writer claims that moving city elections to November would increase turnout. Which additional information would provide the strongest support for this claim?
options: A list of the people currently serving on the Riverton city council
A neighbor's statement that she enjoys voting in May because the lines are short
The cost of printing ballots for a May election
Turnout figures from similar cities before and after they moved local elections to November
items.explain: The claim is about cause and effect: moving the date will raise turnout. The best evidence would show what actually happened to turnout in comparable cities that made the same change. A list of council members and the cost of ballots do not address turnout, and one neighbor's preference is a single personal opinion that, if anything, points the other way.

items.skill: U.S. history: point of view in a primary source
items.prompt: Which statement best describes how Jackson presents the removal policy in the excerpt?
options: As a generous policy that will benefit Native Americans as well as the United States
As a harsh punishment for Native nations that had attacked the government
As a temporary policy that Congress should soon reverse
As a decision that Native nations made without any role for the government
items.explain: Jackson calls the policy "benevolent" and says its success is "a happy consummation." He claims it will help "the Indians themselves" as well as the United States and the states. This reflects his point of view as the leader carrying out the policy; it leaves out the fact that many Native nations opposed removal. He does not describe the policy as punishment or as temporary, and he stresses the role of "the Government."

items.skill: U.S. history: evidence from a primary source
items.prompt: According to Jackson, which are benefits that removal would bring to Native Americans themselves? Select two answers.
options: It would separate them from immediate contact with white settlements.
It would free them from the power of the states.
It would place a dense population of settlers on lands they had occupied.
It would give them seats in Congress to represent their interests.
It would make them citizens of the states where they had lived.
items.explain: Jackson says removal "will separate the Indians from immediate contact with settlements of whites; free them from the power of the States." He presents both as benefits to Native Americans. Placing "a dense and civilized population" on the land is a benefit he names for the United States and its settlers, not for the Native nations being removed. The excerpt says nothing about seats in Congress or state citizenship.

items.prompt: Which later event was a direct result of the policy described in the excerpt?
options: The Louisiana Purchase
The Trail of Tears
The Lewis and Clark expedition
The Missouri Compromise
items.explain: Under the Indian Removal Act, the federal government pressured Native nations of the Southeast to give up their homelands. In 1838 and 1839, the U.S. Army forced the Cherokee to move to Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma), and thousands died on the journey known as the Trail of Tears. The Louisiana Purchase (1803), the Lewis and Clark expedition (1804–1806), and the Missouri Compromise (1820) all happened before Jackson's 1830 message, so none could be a result of it.

items.prompt: Based on the date of the message and the introduction, what was Roosevelt most likely trying to do?
options: Announce that the United States had declared war on Japan
Persuade Americans that the nation should stay out of all world affairs
Build support for helping nations that were resisting aggression, before the United States entered the war
Propose a constitutional amendment adding freedom from want to the Bill of Rights
items.explain: In January 1941 the United States was not yet at war; it entered World War II after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941. Roosevelt's vision of freedom "everywhere in the world" and a world in which no nation could commit "physical aggression against any neighbor" was meant to rally Americans to support nations such as Great Britain; Congress passed the Lend-Lease Act to supply them two months later. The war with Japan began later that year, the message looks outward rather than urging isolation, and it did not propose an amendment.

items.skill: U.S. history: connecting documents to the Constitution
items.prompt: Some of Roosevelt's Four Freedoms are already protected for Americans by the First Amendment, which bars Congress from making laws that limit free speech or the free exercise of religion. Others are broader goals that do not appear in the Bill of Rights. Drag each freedom into the correct category.
choices: Freedom of every person to worship God in his own way
bins: A goal not stated in the Bill of Rights
items.explain: The First Amendment protects freedom of speech and the free exercise of religion, so the first two freedoms belong in that category. Freedom from want (economic security for every nation) and freedom from fear (a worldwide reduction of armaments so that no nation can attack its neighbors) are international goals Roosevelt described; no amendment in the Bill of Rights guarantees them.

items.skill: U.S. history: main idea of a primary source
items.prompt: Which statement best expresses Eisenhower's main idea in the excerpt?
options: The United States should end its arms industry because it is no longer needed.
Military leaders, rather than citizens, should decide how much the nation spends on defense.
The United States should rely only on alliances with other nations for its defense.
Citizens and government must stay alert so that the combined power of the military and the arms industry does not threaten liberty.
items.explain: Eisenhower warns that the "military-industrial complex" could gain "unwarranted influence" and that "only an alert and knowledgeable citizenry" can keep defense in balance with liberty. He does not call for ending the arms industry—he says "we recognize the imperative need for this development"—and he puts responsibility on citizens, not only on military leaders. Alliances are not mentioned.

items.prompt: Which statement about Eisenhower's view of the large military establishment is best supported by the excerpt?
options: He considered it necessary but believed it could become dangerous if it were not watched carefully.
He believed it had already taken over the federal government.
He considered it a temporary arrangement that would end once he left office.
He believed it affected only military bases and had little effect on ordinary communities.
items.explain: Eisenhower writes, "We recognize the imperative need for this development. Yet we must not fail to comprehend its grave implications." He accepts the military establishment as necessary during the Cold War while warning of "the potential for the disastrous rise of misplaced power." He speaks of a potential danger, not a takeover that has already happened; he says the danger "will persist"; and he says its influence "is felt in every city." His background as a general makes his warning especially notable.

items.prompt: By what percent did Country R's real GDP fall from its highest point in Year 1 to its lowest point in Year 2? Round to the nearest tenth of a percent.
items.explain:
Highest point (peak): Y1 Q4, $520 billion.
Lowest point (trough): Y2 Q3, $490 billion.
Decrease: 520 − 490 = 30
Percent decrease: 30 ÷ 520 = 0.05769 ≈ 5.8%
A common error is dividing by the lower value (30 ÷ 490 ≈ 6.1%). Percent change is always measured from the starting value.

items.prompt:
Complete the statement.

From Year 1, Quarter 4 to Year 2, Quarter 3, Country R's real GDP fell for three quarters in a row. This phase of the business cycle is called a(n) {{0}}. The lowest point of real GDP, in Year 2, Quarter 3, is called the {{1}}. During the months when output was falling, the unemployment rate most likely {{2}}.

options: contraction
expansion
peak
equilibrium
peak
trough
surplus
expansion
rose
fell
dropped to zero
stayed exactly the same

items.explain: The business cycle has four phases: expansion, peak, contraction, and trough. When real GDP falls, the economy is in a contraction (a contraction that lasts two or more quarters is commonly called a recession). The lowest point before growth resumes is the trough. When businesses produce less, they need fewer workers, so unemployment usually rises during a contraction. A peak is the highest point, which Country R reached in Year 1, Quarter 4.

items.prompt: Between which two quarters did Country R's real GDP increase by the greatest amount?
options: From Y1 Q1 to Y1 Q2
From Y2 Q4 to Y3 Q1
From Y3 Q2 to Y3 Q3
From Y3 Q3 to Y3 Q4
items.explain:
Find each change:
Y1 Q1 to Y1 Q2: 508 − 500 = 8
Y2 Q4 to Y3 Q1: 503 − 494 = 9
Y3 Q2 to Y3 Q3: 522 − 512 = 10
Y3 Q3 to Y3 Q4: 530 − 522 = 8
The largest one-quarter increase, $10 billion, came from Y3 Q2 to Y3 Q3.

items.prompt: Suppose Country R's government wanted to use fiscal policy to help the economy recover during Year 2. Which action would it most likely take?
options: The central bank lowers interest rates to encourage borrowing.
The legislature cuts income taxes and increases spending on public works projects.
The legislature raises taxes to reduce the government's debt.
The government cuts spending on roads and schools.
items.explain: Fiscal policy is the government's use of taxing and spending. To fight a contraction, expansionary fiscal policy lowers taxes and/or raises government spending, putting more money into the economy. Lowering interest rates is monetary policy, carried out by a central bank, not fiscal policy. Raising taxes or cutting spending would reduce demand, which is the opposite of what an expansionary policy does.

items.prompt: Which transaction would be counted in Country R's GDP for this year?
options: A family sells its used car to a neighbor.
An investor buys shares of stock in a company.
A parent cooks dinner for the family at home without pay.
A household buys a new washing machine made in a Country R factory this year.
items.explain: GDP counts the market value of final goods and services newly produced within the country. A new washing machine made in Country R this year and sold to a household is a newly produced final good, so it counts. A used car was counted when it was first produced, so reselling it adds nothing new. Buying stock is a financial transaction, not production of a good or service. Unpaid work at home is not sold in a market, so it is not counted.

items.prompt: According to the table, in which census year did more than half of the U.S. population first live in urban areas?
items.explain: "More than half" means above 50 percent. In 1900 the urban share was 39.6%, still below half. In 1920 it reached 51.2%, the first year in the table above 50%. By 1940 it was already 56.5%, but 1920 came first.

items.prompt: By how many percentage points did the share of the U.S. population living in urban areas increase from 1880 to 1920?
items.explain:
1920: 51.2%
1880: 28.2%
51.2 − 28.2 = 23.0 percentage points.
A common error is reading the wrong year, such as 1900 (51.2 − 39.6 = 11.6).

items.prompt: Which factors help explain the rapid growth of the U.S. urban population between 1880 and 1920? Select two answers.
options: New factory and industrial jobs were concentrated in cities.
Millions of immigrants arriving from Europe settled in cities.
The Interstate Highway System made it easy to commute from the suburbs.
The Homestead Act offered free farmland to settlers in the West.
Home air conditioning made cities in hot climates more comfortable.
items.explain: Between 1880 and 1920, industrialization created millions of factory jobs in cities, and a huge wave of immigrants, mostly from Europe, settled in cities such as New York and Chicago. Both pulled people into urban areas. The Interstate Highway System (begun in 1956) and home air conditioning (widespread after 1950) came later. The Homestead Act encouraged people to settle on farms, which would draw people toward rural areas, not cities.

items.prompt: In 2020, the world's population was about as urban as the U.S. population had been in which census year?
items.explain: In 2020, about 56% of the world's population lived in urban areas. The U.S. urban share was 56.5% in 1940, the closest match. In 1880 it was 28.2%, in 1960 69.9%, and in 1980 73.7%, all far from 56%. This comparison shows that the United States urbanized much earlier than the world as a whole.

items.prompt: In the mid-1900s, new tractors and other farm machines allowed fewer workers to farm the same amount of land, and many rural workers moved to cities to look for jobs. For these workers, farm machinery was an example of a
options: push factor, because it gave people a reason to leave the places where they lived
pull factor, because it attracted people to the cities
physical barrier, because it made migration more difficult
natural increase, because it raised the birth rate in cities
items.explain: A push factor is a condition that drives people away from a place. Farm machines reduced the number of farm jobs, pushing workers out of rural areas. Job openings in cities would be pull factors, attracting people to a place; the machines themselves did not attract anyone to cities. Farm machinery did not block migration or change birth rates.
